title: Function types, lambdas and closures
goal: By the end you can store, pass and return functions as values, read any Kotlin function type, predict what a lambda or reference compiles to, and explain why a captured var shared between threads loses updates.

warmup.q: `fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0; return { ++count } }`. Four threads share one counter and call it 250,000 times each. What does the next call return?
options: It doesn't compile: Kotlin, like Java, won't let a lambda change a captured local
Often less than 1,000,001, and a different number from run to run
Always 250,001, because each thread gets its own copy of count
warmup.why: Kotlin does let a lambda change a captured `var`. It moves `count` into a heap object, a `Ref$IntRef` with one plain `int` field, that all four threads share. `++count` is a read, an add and a write on that field, so increments get lost when two threads read the same old value. Java would refuse to compile the same code; Kotlin compiles it and races.

sections.h: What a lambda turns into on the JVM
sections.body:
A function value is an object, so something has to create it. What that costs depends on how you wrote it, and Kotlin and Java don't agree on every case.

Since **Kotlin 2.0, lambdas compile to `invokedynamic`** by default, the mechanism Java has used for lambdas since Java 8. The compiler moves the lambda body into a private static method, such as `nonCapturing$lambda$0`. At the place where the lambda is created, it emits an `invokedynamic` instruction whose bootstrap method is `LambdaMetafactory.metafactory`. The first time that instruction runs, the JVM spins up a hidden class that implements `Function1` and calls the private method. No `.class` file for the lambda shows up in your build output. (Kotlin 1.x generated one class per lambda, and the compiler flag `-Xlambdas=class` still brings that back.)

How many objects you get depends on what the lambda captures:

```java
nonCapturing() == nonCapturing();       // true: one shared instance
capturing(30) == capturing(30);         // false: a new object per evaluation
```

```kotlin
nonCapturing() === nonCapturing()       // true: one shared instance
capturing(30) === capturing(30)         // false: a new object per evaluation
capturing(30) == capturing(30)          // false: lambdas have no equals
```

A **non-capturing** lambda uses nothing from outside its body, so one instance serves every call. A **capturing** lambda holds the values it uses (`feeCents` here), so each evaluation allocates a new object with those values inside.

Function references are where Kotlin differs from Java. In Kotlin 2.4.21, `::addFee` and `m::withFee` still compile to real classes, `LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1` and `LambdaShapesKt$boundRef$1`, which extend `kotlin.jvm.internal.FunctionReferenceImpl`. An unbound reference is a singleton held in a static `INSTANCE` field. A bound one is a new object each time, holding its receiver. Java method references go through `invokedynamic` like lambdas do, and leave no class file behind.

One more cost hides in the types. `(Long) -> Long` is `Function1<Long, Long>`, which is generic, so a call through it boxes the `long` into a `java.lang.Long` and back. Java avoids that with primitive interfaces like `LongUnaryOperator`. Kotlin has no primitive function interfaces. It avoids the box another way, with `inline` functions, which the next lesson covers.

None of this is a reason to avoid lambdas. A capturing lambda costs one small object per evaluation, which the JVM allocates cheaply. It starts to matter in two places: a capturing lambda created inside a hot loop, and code that compares function values with `==`, which never works for lambdas.

try.title: Count the objects and the class files
steps: Run `LambdaShapes` (or `LambdaShapesJava`). Before you look, predict the five `true` or `false` answers.
From `labs/`, list the compiled demo classes: `ls functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/`. Look for a class per lambda and a class per reference.
Run `javap -c -p functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/LambdaShapesKt.class` and find the first instruction of `nonCapturing` and of `topLevelRef`.

code.title: LambdaShapes.kt
code.src:
package workbench.functional.l02.demo

fun addFee(cents: Long): Long = cents + 30

fun nonCapturing(): (Long) -> Long = { it + 30 }               // uses nothing from outside
fun capturing(feeCents: Long): (Long) -> Long = { it + feeCents } // captures feeCents
fun topLevelRef(): (Long) -> Long = ::addFee                   // a function reference

class Merchant(private val feeCents: Long) {
    fun withFee(cents: Long): Long = cents + feeCents
}

fun boundRef(m: Merchant): (Long) -> Long = m::withFee          // a reference bound to one object

fun main() {
    val m = Merchant(30)
    println("non-capturing lambda: same object every time?  ${nonCapturing() === nonCapturing()}")
    println("capturing lambda: same object every time?      ${capturing(30) === capturing(30)}")
    println("capturing lambdas equal with == ?              ${capturing(30) == capturing(30)}")
    println("unbound reference ::addFee: same object?       ${topLevelRef() === topLevelRef()}")
    println("bound reference m::withFee: same object?       ${boundRef(m) === boundRef(m)}")
    println()
    val lambda = nonCapturing().javaClass
    val ref = topLevelRef().javaClass
    println("lambda class:    ${lambda.name}  (hidden: ${lambda.isHidden})")
    println("reference class: ${ref.name}  (hidden: ${ref.isHidden}, extends ${ref.superclass.simpleName})")
}

alt.title: LambdaShapesJava.java

try.expect: `true, false, false, true, false` in both languages. The Kotlin lambda's class is a hidden class named like `LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x...`, while the reference's class is an ordinary class, `LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1`, that extends `FunctionReferenceImpl`. The directory has `LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1.class` and `LambdaShapesKt$boundRef$1.class`, and no file for any lambda. In the Java version, the lambda and the method reference are both hidden classes. `javap` shows `invokedynamic ... invoke:()Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1;` in `nonCapturing` and `getstatic ... LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1.INSTANCE` in `topLevelRef`.

sections.h: A closure keeps its variables, and a captured var is a shared box
sections.body:
A lambda can use variables from the function that created it, and it keeps them after that function has returned. Code plus the variables it captured is called a **closure**.

```java
static IntSupplier makeCounter() {
    int[] count = {0};                  // Java makes you build the box yourself
    return () -> ++count[0];
}
```

```kotlin
fun makeCounter(): () -> Int {
    var count = 0
    return { ++count }                  // the lambda keeps count alive
}
```

Call `makeCounter()` twice and you get two counters, each with its own `count`. Each one returns 1, 2, 3 and so on.

Look at what the Java version needed. Java refuses to capture a local variable that changes: `local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final`. The reason is mechanical. A local variable lives in the method's stack frame, and that frame is gone once `makeCounter` returns. The lambda outlives it, so all it can take is a copy of the value, and copying a variable that keeps changing would be confusing. Java programmers work around it with a one-element array or an `AtomicInteger`: an object on the heap that both sides point to.

Kotlin builds that object for you, silently. When a lambda captures a `var`, the compiler moves the variable into a small heap object, `kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref$IntRef` (or `LongRef`, `ObjectRef` and so on), and both the function and the lambda use its field. The field is a plain `public int element`, with no `volatile` and no lock.

That's fine on one thread. It's a bug as soon as two threads share the closure. `++count` becomes "read `element`, add one, write `element`", the same read-modify-write as `count++` in the race conditions lesson, and updates get lost. Nothing in the Kotlin source looks shared. The sharing comes from the box the compiler made.

There are two fixes. Share a thread-safe object instead of a `var`: capture `val count = AtomicLong()` and call `count.incrementAndGet()`. Or, better, don't share at all. Let each task count its own work and combine the results at the end with a sum or a `fold`. The second fix is the functional one, and it keeps working when the tasks move to other machines.

try.title: Lose updates, then fix it two ways
steps: Run `CapturedRace` (or `CapturedRaceJava`). Four pool threads each add 1 to a captured `total` 250,000 times, ten runs in a row.
Fix it by sharing a thread-safe object: make it `val total = AtomicLong()` (Java: `AtomicLong total = new AtomicLong()`), call `total.incrementAndGet()` in the loop, and print `total.get()`. Run it.

Undo that, and fix it by not sharing: make each task return its own count, `pool.submit(Callable { go.await(); var mine = 0L; repeat(250_000) { mine += 1 }; mine })`, then add up `tasks.sumOf { it.get() }`. (Java: return `mine` from the lambda and add up the `Future<Long>` results.) Run it.

refs.title: Ref.java: the boxes for captured vars (Kotlin stdlib source)

analogy: A closure is a pocket calculator you take home from the office with a number still in its memory. The office, the function that made it, has closed for the day, but the number goes where the calculator goes. Two colleagues can each take their own calculator and keep separate totals. The trouble starts when two people share one calculator and both press M+ at the same moment: each reads the memory, adds, and writes back, and one press disappears. The analogy breaks because a real calculator takes one key press at a time. A `Ref` box has no such protection.
in_your_world: Rules as values fit the per-merchant configuration your payment service already has. Build a `Map<MerchantTier, List<Rule>>` once at startup in an `@ApplicationScoped` Quarkus bean, look up the list on each authorization, and run it. Kafka consumers are where closures bite. A `var processed = 0` captured by the handler lambda of a listener running with concurrency 4 is one `Ref` box shared by four threads, and your metric undercounts under load. Use a Micrometer counter or a `LongAdder` for shared counts, and keep per-message state inside the handler. A Temporal activity retried on another worker never sees the closure at all, so don't keep business state in one.
mistake: The common mistake is changing a captured `var` from a lambda that runs somewhere else: a callback, a `CompletableFuture` stage, a pool task, a parallel stream. Kotlin compiles it without a word, because capturing a `var` is legal; the variable just becomes a `Ref` box with a plain field. Java stops you with the effectively-final error, and then people reach for `long[] total = {0}`, which is the same box with the same race. Don't accumulate through shared state. Return a value from each task and combine the values (`sum`, `fold`). If you really need one live shared count, capture a `val` that holds an `AtomicLong` or a `LongAdder`.

compare.title: Rules and closures with functional interfaces and with function types

java.title: Rules.java

kotlin.title: Rules.kt

compare.note: Kotlin has function types; Java has functional interfaces. That changes three things you notice every day. Kotlin calls a function value with `f(x)`, where Java needs the interface's method name (`apply`, `test`, `getAsInt`), and Kotlin has one family of types, `(A) -> B`, where Java has dozens of interfaces, primitive ones included. Kotlin's types can say "may be null" (`Rejection?`, `((Rejection) -> Unit)?`), so a rule that returns null shows it in its type. And Kotlin lets a lambda capture a `var` by moving it into a `Ref` box, where Java insists on effectively final locals and makes you write the box. Under the hood both compile lambdas with `invokedynamic`; only Kotlin's function references still compile to classes.

worked.title: Find the hidden shared box in a settlement job

steps.say: A settlement job posts payments to the ledger in chunks of 500 on a thread pool and adds up what it settled. Under load the total comes out a little low, and only sometimes. Find the shared state before reading on.

1. Find the box. `settledCents` is a `var` captured by the lambda passed to `submit`, which runs on pool threads. The compiler turned it into one `Ref$LongRef`, and every chunk task does read, add, write on its plain `element` field. (`forEach` is inline, so its lambda doesn't count; the `submit` lambda is the one that captures.) Java refused the same code, and the usual Java workaround is the same box written by hand.
steps.alt_code:
long[] settledCents = {0};                                 // the box Java makes you write
pool.submit(() -> { ...; settledCents[0] += p.amountCents(); }); // the same race

steps.say: 2. Don't share. Make each task return its own subtotal, and add the subtotals up on the calling thread. Each task's lambda now captures only its `chunk`, which nobody changes. Self-check: why is `sumOf` inside the task safe? (It runs on one thread over that task's own chunk, and its running total is a local.)

3. If you really need a live shared number, say a progress gauge while the job runs, share a thread-safe object through a `val`, never a `var`. `LongAdder` spreads the contention over several cells and is cheaper than `AtomicLong` when many threads add at once.
steps.code:
val settledSoFar = LongAdder()                 // a val: the reference never changes
pool.submit { chunk.forEach { p -> if (ledger.post(p)) settledSoFar.add(p.amountCents) } }
steps.alt_code:
LongAdder settledSoFar = new LongAdder();      // effectively final, so Java is happy too
pool.submit(() -> { for (Payment p : chunk) if (ledger.post(p)) settledSoFar.add(p.amountCents()); });

drill.title: Write two closures from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `feeRule(percent, minCents)`, which returns a function from an amount in cents to a fee: `amount * percent / 100`, but never less than `minCents`. Then write `makeCounter()`, and add a one-line comment saying what the compiler does with its captured `var`. Write both in Kotlin and in Java, and note the one line Java refuses to compile.

recap: A function type such as `(Payment) -> Rejection?` is a type like any other: store its values, put them in lists, pass them and return them. On the JVM it is `Function1`.
Java uses functional interfaces (`Function`, `Predicate`, your own) and calls them by method name. Kotlin calls a function value like a function.
Lambdas, anonymous functions, references and classes that implement a function type all make function values. A bare `return` is prohibited in a lambda that isn't inlined.

Kotlin 2.x compiles lambdas with `invokedynamic`: no class file, one shared instance when nothing is captured, a new object per evaluation when something is. Function references still compile to classes.
A closure keeps the variables it captured. A captured `var` lives in a `Ref` box with a plain field, so a closure shared between threads loses updates.
Share a `val` that holds an atomic or, better, return a value from each task and combine the values.

quiz.q: `fun cap(fee: Long): (Long) -> Long = { it + fee }`. What do `println(cap(30) === cap(30))` and `println(cap(30)(100) == cap(30)(100))` print?
quiz.why: The lambda captures `fee`, so every evaluation creates a new object, and `===` compares objects. Calling both gives `130`, and two `Long` values compare equal with `==`. A lambda that captured nothing would print `true` for the first line, because one shared instance serves every call.

quiz.q: Which parameter declaration means "an optional callback that receives a Rejection"?
quiz.why: The parentheses make the whole function type nullable, so the caller may pass nothing and you call it with `onReject?.invoke(r)`. Without them, `(Rejection) -> Unit?` is a required function that returns `Unit?`. The second takes a nullable argument, and the third is a function with a receiver.

quiz.q: In Kotlin 2.4.21, which of these leaves a `.class` file of its own in your build output?
options: `::isServed`, a reference to a top-level function
quiz.why: Function references still compile to a class extending `FunctionReferenceImpl`; an unbound one is a singleton. Lambdas, capturing or not, and SAM conversions like `Runnable { }` compile to `invokedynamic`, and the JVM creates a hidden class at runtime, with no file on disk. Capturing changes how many objects you get, not whether a class file exists.

quiz.q: A Kafka listener runs with concurrency 4. Its handler is a lambda that does `processed++` on a captured `var processed = 0`. What happens to `processed`?
options: It's exact, because Kotlin makes captured vars thread-safe
It doesn't compile, just like in Java
It can end up lower than the number of messages, because all four threads share one plain field in a `Ref` box
Each thread gets its own copy, so it counts only one thread's messages
quiz.why: Kotlin allows the capture and moves the variable into one `Ref$IntRef` on the heap. All four threads run read, add, write on its non-volatile `element` field, so increments get lost. Java would reject the code; Kotlin compiles it. Use a `LongAdder` or a metrics counter.

quiz.q: From the contravariance lesson: `Function1` is declared `Function1<in P1, out R>`. Can you put `val logAll: (Any) -> Rejection? = { null }` into a `List<Rule>`, where `Rule = (Payment) -> Rejection?`?
options: Yes: a function that accepts any object can certainly accept a Payment
No: `Any` is not `Payment`, so the types don't match
quiz.why: The parameter type of a function is an in-position, and `Function1` is contravariant in it: `(Any) -> R` is a subtype of `(Payment) -> R` because every `Payment` is an `Any`. The return type is covariant. The tempting "no" applies the subtype arrow the wrong way round, which is exactly what `in` fixes.

flashcards.front: What JVM interface does Kotlin's `(Payment) -> Rejection?` compile to?
flashcards.back: `kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Payment, Rejection>`. Calling the value calls its `invoke` method.

flashcards.front: How do you declare an optional callback that takes a Rejection?
flashcards.back: `onReject: ((Rejection) -> Unit)? = null`, with the parentheses, and call it with `onReject?.invoke(r)`.

flashcards.front: In Kotlin 2.x, is `nonCapturing() === nonCapturing()` true for a lambda that captures nothing?
flashcards.back: Yes. The `invokedynamic` call site hands out one shared instance. A capturing lambda is a new object each time.
No. Function references still compile to a class that extends `FunctionReferenceImpl`; an unbound one is a singleton `INSTANCE`.

flashcards.front: What does a `var` captured by a lambda become?
flashcards.back: A `kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref` box (`IntRef`, `LongRef`, `ObjectRef`) with a plain, non-volatile `element` field.

flashcards.front: Why won't `{ cents -> if (cents < 0) return true; cents > 0 }` compile?
flashcards.back: A bare `return` returns from the enclosing `fun`, which is only allowed when the lambda is inlined: `'return' is prohibited here.` Use `return@label` or an anonymous function.

flashcards.front: What does javac say when a lambda changes a captured local?
flashcards.back: `local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final`.

terms.plain: A type for functions, like `(Payment) -> Rejection?`. Its values can be stored, passed and returned.
A function value written inline: `{ p -> p.amountCents > 0 }`.
A named function used as a value: `::isServed`, `Payment::isDomestic`, `limits::check`.
Java's stand-in for a function type: an interface with one abstract method, like `Function<T, R>`.
A function value together with the variables it captured from the place it was created.
A lambda that uses values from outside its body, so each evaluation creates a new object that holds them.
The small heap object (`Ref$IntRef` and friends) that the Kotlin compiler puts a captured `var` into.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's Kotlin counter, a `var n = 0` captured by a lambda that four threads call, loses counts. They say: "There's no shared field anywhere in my code." Explain what the compiler did and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: A local variable normally lives in the stack frame of the function that declares it, and the lambda outlives that frame. So when a lambda captures a `var`, Kotlin moves the variable into a small object on the heap, a `Ref$IntRef`, and both the function and the lambda use its `element` field. That field is the shared field: all four threads reach it through the same lambda. It's a plain field, so `n++` is a read, an add and a write that two threads can interleave, and increments get lost. Java would have refused to compile the capture. I'd stop sharing: have each thread or task count its own work and add the counts up at the end. If a live shared count is really needed, I'd capture a `val` holding a `LongAdder` or `AtomicLong` instead of a `var`.

deeper.body:
`javap -v` shows how `invokedynamic` is wired. Each lambda site has an entry in the class's `BootstrapMethods` table pointing at `LambdaMetafactory.metafactory`, with three arguments: the erased method type of `invoke`, `(Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;`, a handle to the private static method holding the body, and the instantiated type, `(Ljava/lang/Long;)Ljava/lang/Long;` for a `(Long) -> Long`. The erased signature is why a call through `Function1` boxes: `invoke` takes and returns `Object`.

Kotlin 2.0's switch to `invokedynamic` changed three visible things, according to its release notes. These lambdas aren't serializable, the experimental `reflect()` API doesn't support them, and `toString()` prints the hidden class name, something like `LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x...@1b6d3586`, instead of a readable description of the function type. A test or log that matched on the old text breaks after the upgrade. Annotate a single lambda with `@JvmSerializableLambda`, or compile the module with `-Xlambdas=class`, to get the old class-per-lambda behaviour.

SAM conversions went to `invokedynamic` earlier, in Kotlin 1.5. That covers a Kotlin lambda passed where Java expects a `Runnable` or `Comparator`, and a lambda for your own `fun interface`:

```kotlin
fun interface FeeRule { fun feeFor(amountCents: Long): Long }

val flat = FeeRule { 30 }                  // a SAM conversion: invokedynamic, no class file
val task = Runnable { println("settled") } // the same for a Java interface
```

```java
@FunctionalInterface
interface FeeRule { long feeFor(long amountCents); }

FeeRule flat = amountCents -> 30;              // Java lambdas have always worked this way
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("settled");
```

A `fun interface` is worth using when a function type needs a name in a public API, or when Java callers will implement it, since Java code can't write a lambda for `Function1` as naturally as for an interface named after its job.
